answer_text:
Let

\[
f \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Z})
\]

be a group homomorphism between the additive groups \(\mathbb{Q}\) and \(\mathbb{Z}\).

Since \(1 \in \mathbb{Q}\), set

\[
f(1)=n
\]

for some integer \(n\).

For any positive integer \(m\), we have

\[
m \cdot \frac{1}{m}=1.
\]

Applying \(f\),

\[
f\left(m \cdot \frac{1}{m}\right)=m f\left(\frac{1}{m}\right)=f(1)=n.
\]

Thus \(n\) must be divisible by every positive integer \(m\) inside \(\mathbb{Z}\). The only integer divisible by every positive integer is \(0\). Hence

\[
f(1)=0.
\]

Now take any rational number \(q=\frac{a}{b}\), where \(a,b \in \mathbb{Z}\) and \(b \neq 0\). Then

\[
b f\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)
= f(a)
= a f(1)
= a \cdot 0
= 0.
\]

Since \(\mathbb{Z}\) has no torsion, \(b f\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)=0\) implies

\[
f\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)=0.
\]

Therefore \(f(q)=0\) for every \(q \in \mathbb{Q}\). Hence every homomorphism is the zero map, so

\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Z}) \cong 0.
\]

\[
\boxed{0}
\]
